conventional_description: In Western medicine, food poisoning is an illness caused by eating contaminated food. Bacteria, viruses, parasites, or their toxins irritate the lining of the stomach and intestines, leading to nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and sometimes fever. Diagnosis is usually based on symptoms and a history of recent food intake; stool tests may be done in severe or persistent cases. Most cases resolve on their own within a few days with rest and hydration.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment focuses on preventing dehydration and managing symptoms. This typically includes drinking plenty of fluids, oral rehydration solutions, and rest. Over-the-counter anti-diarrheal medications may be used cautiously, but they are often avoided if there is fever or bloody stools. In bacterial cases, antibiotics may be prescribed, and antiemetics can help control severe nausea and vomiting.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands food poisoning as an invasion of external toxins that disrupt the Spleen and Stomach, the organs responsible for digestion and fluid metabolism. The Stomach normally sends food downward, while the Spleen transforms it into energy and sends the clear upward. When spoiled or contaminated food enters, this delicate balance is thrown off: Stomach Qi rebels upward causing nausea and vomiting, and Spleen Qi sinks downward causing diarrhea.
The nature of the toxin and your body's response determine which pattern emerges. If the food is simply undigested and stagnant, you get sour belching and a thick tongue coating - that's Food Stagnation. If the toxin generates heat and dampness, you'll see foul diarrhea, a yellow greasy tongue, and a heavy sensation - Damp-Heat. Cold or raw foods can directly damage Spleen Yang, leading to Cold-Damp with watery stools and chills. In severe cases, a virulent toxin can create Toxic-Heat with high fever and bloody stools.
This is why TCM doesn't have one remedy for food poisoning. A formula that clears Damp-Heat would be wrong for someone with Cold-Damp, just as a warming formula would worsen Toxic-Heat. By matching the treatment to the exact pattern, TCM can often resolve symptoms within a day or two, while also strengthening the digestive system to prevent a lingering weakness.
classical_translation: "For food poisoning, use Gua Di San (Melon Stalk Powder) to induce vomiting."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first asks about the onset and what was eaten. Sudden nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea right after a heavy or questionable meal point strongly toward Food Stagnation in the Stomach. The tongue coating is thick and greasy, and the pulse feels slippery and full. This pattern is about undigested food rebelling, so the body tries to expel it upward and downward.
When the diarrhea smells foul and the abdominal pain is cramping with a sensation of heat, the picture shifts to Damp-Heat in the Stomach and Spleen. The tongue shows a yellow, greasy coating, and the pulse is rapid and slippery. A low-grade fever and a heavy, lethargic feeling help separate this from simple food stagnation, because the spoiled food has brewed into internal heat and dampness.
If the diarrhea is watery and accompanied by cold abdominal cramps, chills, and a pale tongue with a white coating, the practitioner considers Cold-Damp invading the Spleen. This often follows eating cold or raw contaminated food. The pulse tends to be slow or tight, and the person lacks the heat signs seen in damp-heat, making the distinction clear.
Severe cases with high fever, bloody stools, and signs of systemic toxicity indicate Toxic-Heat. The tongue is deep red with a thick yellow coating, and the pulse is rapid and forceful. This pattern is an emergency; the body is overwhelmed by virulent toxins, and the practitioner looks for delirium, extreme thirst, and dark urine to confirm the depth of heat invasion.
In some people, food toxins combine with preexisting phlegm-damp, causing Phlegm-Dampness in the Middle-Burner. The chief complaints are chest oppression, persistent nausea, and a thick, greasy tongue coating. Diarrhea may be less explosive, but the heavy, stuck sensation and a slippery pulse tell the practitioner that the problem has lodged deeper in the digestive tract.

patterns.symptoms: ["Sour, rotten-smelling belching", "Epigastric fullness and distension worse with pressure", "Nausea or vomiting of sour, undigested food", "Relief after vomiting", "Foul-smelling flatulence and loose stools with sour odour", "Thick, greasy tongue coating (often curd-like, thickest in centre)"]

patterns.better_with: Vomiting (relieves distension), Light, bland congee, Warm ginger tea, Rest and fasting
patterns.why_this_happens:
When you eat spoiled, contaminated, or simply too much food, your Stomach cannot process it properly. The undigested mass sits and ferments, blocking the normal downward movement of Stomach Qi. Trapped Qi then rebels upward as sour belching and vomiting, while the putrefying food rushes downward as foul-smelling diarrhea.
This is an acute excess pattern-the digestive system is physically overwhelmed, not weakened. The turbid stagnation produces the hallmark thick, greasy tongue coating and a slippery, full pulse.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal body with a thick, greasy, curd-like coating, thickest in the centre. Pulse: slippery (Hua) and full (Shi), most prominent at the right middle (guan) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Food stagnation is a physical obstruction that blocks Stomach Qi from descending. Vomiting forcibly clears the obstruction, giving immediate relief. Light, warm foods place no extra burden on the Stomach and gently support Spleen Qi, allowing the digestive system to recover. Fasting gives the Stomach time to process the accumulated food without adding more. Overeating or heavy, greasy, and cold foods directly worsen the stagnation-they are harder to digest and further impair the Stomach's downward movement. Lying down after eating makes it harder for Qi to descend, trapping the stagnation and increasing bloating.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: During the acute phase, rest your digestion completely-fast for a few hours or sip only warm water or light rice congee. Reintroduce food with small portions of bland, easily digested meals like plain congee, steamed vegetables, or clear broth. Avoid all greasy, fried, dairy, raw, and cold foods until your appetite and tongue coating normalize. Gentle walking after meals can help Qi descend.

patterns.why_this_happens: When contaminated food is consumed, it creates Dampness and Heat directly in the digestive tract. The Spleen and Stomach become overwhelmed and cannot transform or transport properly, so Dampness accumulates and combines with Heat. This disturbs the Intestines, causing foul-smelling, sticky diarrhea, while the rising Heat leads to nausea and a bitter taste in the mouth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red body, possibly swollen with teeth marks, with a thick yellow greasy coating especially at the centre and root. Pulse: Soggy (Ru) and rapid (Shu), often slippery (Hua).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat is aggravated by greasy, fried, and dairy foods because they directly create more Dampness and Heat in the digestive system. Humid weather and overwork weaken the Spleen, making it harder to transform Dampness. Rest, light foods, and warm fluids support the Spleen's ability to clear Dampness and cool the Heat, while peppermint and ginger help settle the Stomach and disperse turbidity.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Drink plenty of warm water or light barley tea to help flush Dampness. Avoid all greasy, fried, dairy, and sugary foods, which create more Dampness. Eat small amounts of easily digested congee with a little ginger to support the Spleen. Rest and avoid heavy exertion until the digestive system recovers.

patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid all cold, raw, and greasy foods until the diarrhea stops. Stick to warm, easy-to-digest meals like plain rice congee or cooked millet. Sip warm ginger tea throughout the day to support Spleen Yang and keep the abdomen covered and warm.

patterns.why_this_happens: When contaminated food carries a particularly virulent toxin, it can directly generate intense Heat and Fire in the Stomach and Intestines. This aggressive Heat burns through the body's protective Qi and penetrates deeper, causing high fever and systemic toxicity. The Heat scorches the blood vessels in the intestines, leading to bloody diarrhea, while rising Heat disturbs the mind, causing restlessness and agitation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with prickly raised papillae (thorns) and a dry yellow coating. Pulse: rapid (shu) and forceful (you li), often full (shi) or overflowing (hong).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Toxic-Heat is an aggressive internal Fire that consumes Yin and damages the blood. Cooling foods and rest help lower the internal temperature and preserve fluids, while spicy, greasy, or heating substances add fuel to the Fire. Stress and overexertion further agitate the Qi and worsen the Heat, so calm and quiet are essential to allow the body to clear the toxin.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Drink plenty of cool fluids like water or light herbal teas to help flush toxins. Eat only bland, easily digested foods such as congee once the acute phase passes. Avoid all spicy, greasy, or fried foods, alcohol, and caffeine until full recovery. Rest is essential to conserve Qi for fighting the toxin.

patterns.why_this_happens: If your digestion is already sluggish and prone to phlegm-dampness, contaminated food adds a toxic burden that your Spleen cannot manage. The Spleen's ability to transform and transport fluids stalls, so dampness thickens into phlegm and blocks the middle of your torso. This creates a heavy, stuck sensation in the chest and stomach, persistent nausea, and a thick greasy coating on the tongue.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale and swollen with teeth marks, thick white greasy coating that looks wet. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and often soft or soggy, especially at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-dampness forms when the Spleen is too weak to transform fluids, and it is worsened by anything cold, raw, or greasy that further burdens digestion. Warm, dry foods and a dry environment help the Spleen warm up and evaporate dampness, while gentle movement moves Qi so that phlegm cannot settle and stagnate.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw, greasy, and dairy foods that produce dampness. Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like congee with a little ginger. Gentle daily movement helps Qi flow and clear phlegm. Use warming kitchen spices such as ginger, cardamom, and a small amount of black pepper.

faqs.question: Can TCM treat food poisoning at home?
faqs.answer: Mild cases of food stagnation or simple indigestion can often be managed at home with rest, ginger tea, and bland congee. However, for more severe symptoms like fever, bloody stools, or inability to keep fluids down, you should seek medical attention immediately. TCM herbal formulas should be prescribed by a qualified practitioner who can identify the correct pattern. Self-prescribing the wrong herbs can make things worse.

faqs.question: What herbs are commonly used for food poisoning?
faqs.answer: It depends on the pattern. For simple food stagnation, Bao He Wan with Shan Zha (hawthorn berry) helps digest the backlog. For Damp-Heat with foul diarrhea, Lian Po Yin uses Huang Lian (coptis) to clear heat and dry dampness. Cold-Damp cases benefit from Huo Xiang Zheng Qi San, which warms and transforms dampness. All these formulas are tailored to the individual and should be taken under guidance.

faqs.question: How quickly does acupuncture work for nausea and vomiting?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture can relieve nausea and vomiting very quickly, often within minutes of needle insertion. Points like Neiguan (PC-6) and Zusanli (ST-36) are particularly effective at calming rebellious Stomach Qi. Many patients feel a reduction in nausea during the session itself. For acute food poisoning, one or two treatments may be enough to settle the stomach.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for children with food poisoning?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be very gentle and effective for children. Acupuncture may be replaced by acupressure or pediatric tuina massage for young children. Herbal dosages are adjusted for the child's weight and constitution. However, children dehydrate faster than adults, so any sign of dehydration or high fever should prompt an immediate visit to a doctor. Always consult a pediatric TCM practitioner.

faqs.question: Can I take TCM herbs with antibiotics?
faqs.answer: In many cases, yes, but it's essential to inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor. Some herbs can interact with antibiotics or alter their effectiveness. Typically, herbs and antibiotics are taken a few hours apart to avoid interactions. Your TCM practitioner will adjust the formula if you are on medication. Never stop prescribed antibiotics without your doctor's approval.

faqs.question: What should I eat while recovering from food poisoning?
faqs.answer: Stick to bland, easy-to-digest foods like plain congee, steamed rice, or well-cooked vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, greasy, spicy, or dairy-heavy foods, as they burden the weakened Spleen and Stomach. Warm ginger tea can help settle nausea and warm the digestive system. Gradually reintroduce normal foods as your appetite returns and your stools normalize.

research.title: Huo Xiang Zheng Qi San for acute gastroenteritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: A meta-analysis of 12 RCTs involving 1,245 patients found that Huo Xiang Zheng Qi San, alone or combined with conventional treatment, significantly improved total effective rate and reduced time to resolution of diarrhoea and vomiting compared to conventional treatment alone. Adverse events were minimal.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, et al. Huo Xiang Zheng Qi San for acute gastroenteritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Chinese Journal of Integrative Medicine. 2018;24(7):534-540.

research.title: Acupuncture for acute diarrhoea in adults: a Cochrane systematic review
research.description: This Cochrane review evaluated acupuncture for acute diarrhoea and found that acupuncture may reduce the duration of diarrhoea and improve stool frequency compared to no treatment or sham acupuncture, but the evidence was of low certainty due to small sample sizes and risk of bias.
research.periodical: Liang L, et al. Acupuncture for acute diarrhoea in adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019;Issue 7. Art. No.: CD013275.

research.title: Antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activities of Huang Lian Jie Du Tang and its relevance to foodborne illness
research.description: An in vitro study demonstrated that Huang Lian Jie Du Tang and its major alkaloids (berberine, baicalin) inhibited growth of common foodborne pathogens including Salmonella and Staphylococcus aureus, and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production in intestinal epithelial cells.
research.periodical: Li X, et al. Antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activities of a traditional Chinese herbal formula Huang-Lian-Jie-Du-Tang. Scientific Reports. 2017;7:15733.
